title: Judges 6:11–24
context: Judges 6:11–24 narrates Gideon’s call. The LORD’s angel finds Gideon threshing wheat in a wine press to hide it from Midian and greets him as a mighty man of valor. Gideon questions why the LORD has allowed this, protests his family’s weakness and asks for a sign. Fire from the rock consumes his offering, and Gideon, terrified at having seen the LORD’s angel face to face, is told he will not die. He builds an altar called "The LORD is Peace." The text moves between "the LORD’s angel" and "the LORD," and many interpreters in both traditions read the figure as the LORD himself appearing. Both stress God’s patient, gracious initiative toward a fearful man.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel came and sat under the oak which was in Ophrah, that belonged to Joash the Abiezrite. His son Gideon was beating out wheat in the wine press, to hide it from the Midianites.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s angel sits under the oak at Ophrah, where Gideon is threshing wheat in a wine press to hide it from Midian. Arminian readers see God coming to a man in hiding and in fear, showing that God’s call often comes in unlikely circumstances.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the irony of threshing in a wine press, a hollow place unsuited to the task. Both traditions see the LORD taking the initiative to seek out his chosen deliverer before Gideon seeks him.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel appeared to him, and said to him, “The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor!”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s angel greets Gideon, "The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor!" Arminians read the greeting as God speaking to what Gideon can become through his presence, calling him to respond in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that the title rests on the LORD’s presence, not on Gideon’s existing courage. Both traditions see God’s word creating what it names and see the greeting as gracious, given to a man who is hiding.

verses.text: Gideon said to him, “Oh, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? Where are all his wondrous works which our fathers told us of, saying, ‘Didn’t the LORD bring us up from Egypt?’ But now the LORD has cast us off, and delivered us into the hand of Midian.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon asks why, if the LORD is with them, all this has happened, and where his wondrous works are. Arminian readers see honest questioning that God does not reject, and they note that Gideon knows the exodus story even as he doubts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Gideon does not connect Israel’s suffering with its sin, although the prophet has just done so (6:10). Both traditions see God patiently answering a hurting and confused man and turning his questions toward a call.

verses.text: The LORD looked at him, and said, “Go in this your might, and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Haven’t I sent you?”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD looks at him and says, "Go in this your might, and save Israel... Haven’t I sent you?" Arminian readers see God’s commission calling for Gideon’s willing obedience, with his "might" coming from being sent by God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the speaker is now named as "the LORD," which supports reading the angel as the LORD himself appearing. Both traditions see Gideon’s strength lying in God’s sending, not in himself.

verses.text: He said to him, “O Lord, how shall I save Israel? Behold, my family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon protests that his family is the poorest in Manasseh and he is the least in his father’s house. The word translated "Lord" here is Adonai. Arminians see Gideon’s honest sense of inadequacy, which God answers with his presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s pattern of choosing the weak, a theme later stated in 1 Corinthians 1:26–29. Both traditions read Gideon’s objection, like Moses’ in Exodus 3–4, as answered by God’s promise rather than by Gideon’s qualifications.

verses.text: The LORD said to him, “Surely I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises, "Surely I will be with you," and says Gideon will strike Midian as one man. Arminians see the promise as the ground of Gideon’s confidence: the outcome is assured by God’s presence, which Gideon must trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that "as one man" means Midian will be defeated as easily as a single opponent. Both traditions read the verse as echoing God’s promise to Moses (Exodus 3:12) and see divine presence as the answer to human weakness.

verses.text: He said to him, “If now I have found favor in your sight, then show me a sign that it is you who talk with me.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon asks for a sign that it is really the LORD speaking. Arminian readers see a reasonable request from someone who wants to be sure of the source of the call, and God’s willingness to answer shows his patience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God condescending to Gideon’s weakness. Both traditions note that this sign concerns who is speaking, which is different from the fleece in 6:36–40, where God has already spoken clearly.

verses.text: Please don’t go away until I come to you, and bring out my present, and lay it before you.” He said, “I will wait until you come back.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon asks the visitor to wait while he brings a present, and he agrees to wait. Arminians see Gideon offering hospitality and perhaps testing the visitor, and they see the LORD’s willingness to wait as gracious patience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The word "present" can also refer to an offering, and Gideon may not yet fully understand who the visitor is. Both traditions read the visitor’s patience as part of God’s gentle dealing with a hesitant man.

verses.text: Gideon went in and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes of an ephah of meal. He put the meat in a basket and he put the broth in a pot, and brought it out to him under the oak, and presented it.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon prepares a young goat and unleavened cakes from an ephah of meal, often estimated at about 22 liters. Arminian readers see the size of the gift as costly generosity in a time of famine, a real sacrifice by a poor family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the costliness of the offering while Midian was taking Israel’s crops. Both traditions see Gideon’s gift as an act of honor that becomes an offering to the LORD in the verses that follow.

verses.text: The angel of God said to him, “Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and lay them on this rock, and pour out the broth.” He did so.
verses.arminianNotes: The angel of God tells him to lay the meat and cakes on the rock and pour out the broth, and Gideon does so. Arminians see the shift from meal to offering, with Gideon obeying a simple instruction before he understands what is about to happen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the rock becoming an altar at the visitor’s word. Both traditions note the text’s alternation between "angel of God" and "LORD’s angel," which belongs to the wider discussion of the angel’s identity.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s angel stretched out the end of the staff that was in his hand, and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes; and fire went up out of the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. Then the LORD’s angel departed out of his sight.
verses.arminianNotes: The angel touches the offering with his staff, fire comes from the rock and consumes it, and he vanishes. Arminian readers see the sign Gideon asked for, given in a way that shows the visitor’s divine power and accepts Gideon’s offering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and compare the fire with other occasions when God accepted sacrifices by fire (Leviticus 9:24; 1 Kings 18:38). Both traditions see the sign as God confirming his call, and see the angel’s departure as completing the revelation.

verses.text: Gideon saw that he was the LORD’s angel; and Gideon said, “Alas, Lord GOD! Because I have seen the LORD’s angel face to face!”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon realizes he has seen the LORD’s angel face to face and cries, "Alas, Lord GOD!" Arminians see the right response to God’s holiness: fear and awe when the reality of God’s presence becomes clear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and connect Gideon’s fear with the biblical theme that no one can see God and live (Exodus 33:20; compare Genesis 32:30). Both traditions read his fear as evidence that he understood he had met God himself in some form.

verses.text: The LORD said to him, “Peace be to you! Don’t be afraid. You shall not die.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, "Peace be to you! Don’t be afraid. You shall not die." Arminian readers see God’s comfort answering Gideon’s fear, showing that God’s holiness comes with mercy toward those he calls.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that Gideon’s safety rests on God’s word of peace. Both traditions see the verse as grace following awe and read God’s reassurance as the foundation of Gideon’s call.

verses.text: Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD, and called it “The LORD is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon builds an altar called "The LORD is Peace," and the Hebrew word is Shalom. Arminians see Gideon responding to grace with worship and with a lasting memorial of what God revealed to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the altar stood in Ophrah "to this day," which marks the account as written later. Both traditions read the name as Gideon’s confession of what he had learned about God, who brings peace and not destruction to his servant.
